title: How to evaluate stock performance before investing as a beginner
description: Looking beyond the stock price: P/E, Dividend Yield, and 5-Year Trends.
content:
Beginners often judge a stock by its share price. 'Amazon is $180, that's expensive!' or 'Ford is $12, that's cheap!' This is wrong. Share price tells you nothing about value; it only tells you the price of one slice of the pizza, not the size of the pizza. To evaluate a stock (or even an index fund), you need to look at valuation metrics. You don't need to be a Wall Street analyst, but understanding three or four key numbers prevents you from buying hype at the top of a bubble.

Key Takeaways

  • P/E Ratio (Price to Earnings): The most important metric. How much are you paying for $1 of earnings? Historical S&P 500 average is ~16-20. Anything >30 is 'expensive' (growth expectation).
  • Dividend Yield: How much cash does it pay you? 2% is standard. 5% is high. 10% is usually a distress signal (yield trap).
  • Revenue Growth: Is the company actually selling more stuff than last year? Earnings can be manipulated; Revenue is harder to fake.
  • Beta: A measure of volatility. Beta > 1 means it moves more than the market. Beta < 1 means it is more stable.

Why It Matters (US Context)

US financial disclosures (10-K, 10-Q) are the gold standard for transparency. You can find all this data for free on Yahoo Finance, Google Finance, or your brokerage app. Never buy a stock without spending 5 minutes looking at the numbers.

The 5-Minute Fundamentals Check

Before buying a ticker, check these.

1. P/E Ratio (Valuation)

Price / Earnings.
If Apple earns $6/share and trades at $180, P/E = 30.
Rule of Thumb: Value stocks are 10-15. Growth stocks are 20-50. If a company has a P/E of 100+, it must grow massively to justify the price. If it has no 'E' (negative earnings), it is speculative.

2. 5-Year Chart (Trend)

Zoom out. Is the line going up?
If it's down 80% in 5 years, it's not 'on sale', it's likely dying. 'Catching a falling knife' is dangerous. Look for steady up-and-to-the-right history.

3. Market Cap (Size)

Price x Shares Outstanding.
Mega Cap ($200B+): Stable (Google, Walmart).
Small Cap (<$2B): Risky, volatile, potential for high growth or bankruptcy.
Know what size you are buying.

Evaluating an ETF

  1. Top 10 Holdings: Look at the ETF's fact sheet. What companies are you actually buying? If you buy a 'Tech ETF', it's probably 20% Apple. Do you already own Apple?
  2. Expense Ratio: The cost. Always aim for <0.10% for core holdings.
  3. Turnover Rate: How often do they trade? High turnover (>50%) generates taxes. Low turnover (<5%) is efficient.
  4. AUM (Assets Under Management): Stick to funds with >$1 Billion. Tiny funds have liquidity issues.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is EPS?

Earnings Per Share. Net Profit divided by share count. If EPS is growing every year, the stock price usually follows.

Should I buy stocks at 52-week lows?

Be careful. Stocks usually hit lows for a reason (bad news). Unless the fundamental business is still strong, 'cheap' stocks can get cheaper.

Do I need to do this for Index Funds?

Not really. That is the beauty of indexing. You accept the market's valuation. You don't need to analyze 500 companies; you just buy the bucket.
